# Workflow config (v1)

Schema for `.tera/workflows/<name>.hcl` config files. Each decodes to `pkg/config.WorkflowBlock` (ADR-026) declaring a DAG of steps with CEL-guarded edges and input mapping. The block label is the workflow name.

| | |
|---|---|
| Registry name | `config/workflows` |
| Regime | persisted |
| Identity regime | `recipe` — the filename stem is the identity; the file declares exactly one resource, and a block label — where the grammar admits one — must equal the stem (ADR-087 D3) |
| Current version | `v1` |
| Supported versions | `v1` |
| HCL block | `workflow` |
| Loader directory | `.tera/workflows/<name>.hcl` |
| Go source | `github.com/kottera/kottera/pkg/config.WorkflowBlock` |
| Served at | `GET /api/v1/schemas/config/workflows/reference` |

## Example

A minimal `workflows`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/workflows/example-workflow.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

workflow "example-workflow" {
  step "example" {
    capability "example-tool" {}
  }
}
```

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | block label | Workflow name. Names beginning "__cap/" are reserved: a work_order_type capability recipe is lowered into a synthesized workflow under that prefix (ADR-081 D6), and an authored block claiming it is rejected. |
| `description` | string | no | — | — | — | — |
| `concurrency` | block | no | — | — | — | — |
| `step` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | — |
| `on_failure` | string | no | — | — | — | Step that runs when the workflow fails. Receives the CEL error context; its output becomes the workflow's failure detail (ADR-081). |
| `on_success` | string | no | — | — | — | Step that runs after the terminal step on success. Side-effect-only: its output never replaces the workflow result and the CEL error context is empty (ADR-081). |

## `step` block

Repeatable.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | block label | — |
| `capability` | block | no | — | — | — | Dispatch this step to a tool capability directly. The block label names the capability. A step declares exactly one target block; the legal set is the derived "exactly one of" section below (ADR-087 D4). |
| `select` | block | no | — | — | — | Dispatch this step to one of a closed set of interchangeable candidates, chosen at admission from the work order's own input (ADR-130 D7). The block takes no label: its references are the candidate blocks' own capability labels. A step declares exactly one target block; the legal set is the derived "exactly one of" section below (ADR-087 D4). |
| `ask` | block | no | — | — | — | Park this run and ask a person a question (ADR-086 D1). The step dispatches to nothing: it parks on arrival, the answer is validated against the step's output_schema and becomes the step's output, and downstream steps read it as steps.<name>.output. The owning work_order_type must be able to park for awaiting-input, which is checked at load time; since ADR-086's 2026-08-31 amendment that reason is derived from the type's structure, so the way to fail the check is an explicit may_pause_for or never_pause_for that subtracts it rather than an omission. A step declares exactly one target block; the legal set is the derived "exactly one of" section below (ADR-087 D4). |
| `child` | block | no | — | — | — | File one Work Order of the named work_order_type as a child of the running Work Order, with this step's resolved input_map as its inputs, and park until that child settles (ADR-138). The block label names the type, resolved once at load: a bare leaf works as it does on tera workorder create --type, and a leaf more than one vault registers is refused naming every candidate. The child type's input_schema and output_schema are this step's contract, so input_schema, output_schema and max_retries are refused on a child step; a completed child's outputs become steps.<name>.output. Not permitted as an on_failure or on_success handler, nor in a workflow bound to a worker responsibility. The owning work_order_type must be able to park for awaiting-event. The block body is empty. A step declares exactly one target block; the legal set is the derived "exactly one of" section below (ADR-087 D4). |
| `condition` | string | no | — | — | — | — |
| `next` | string[] | no | — | — | — | — |
| `input_map` | block | no | — | — | — | — |
| `input_schema` | string | no | — | — | — | — |
| `output_schema` | string | no | — | — | — | — |
| `max_retries` | integer | no | `0` | — | — | Retries for this step *within* one workflow dispatch: the step runs at most max_retries+1 times, re-sending the input resolved before the first attempt (conditions and input_map are never re-evaluated) with no back-off. Default 0 — no retry. A capability step retries transport and tool errors only, never an output_schema failure: re-running a deterministic tool against the same input would just reproduce it. Composes MULTIPLICATIVELY with the Work Order retry ladder, which re-dispatches the whole recipe (ADR-046 defaults.max_retries): max_retries=2 here inside a recipe with max_retries=3 is up to 3x4 = 12 invocations of this step. Budget both. |

**Exactly one of** `capability` | `select` | `ask` | `child`.

## `step.capability` block

Nested under `step`.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | block label | — |
| `operation` | string | no | `invoke` | — | — | Capability operation to invoke. |
| `config` | block | no | — | — | — | Binding config handed to the capability as the invocation's binding_config (ADR-082 D1). String values may reference ${inputs.X} and are substituted against the owning Work Order's spec inputs at dispatch; on a dispatch with no Work Order behind it such a reference is a resolution error, not an empty string. Validated at load against the named tool's config_schema when the tool is resolvable in this configuration. |
| `config_map` | block | no | — | — | — | Typed CEL expressions contributing binding configuration. Expressions see only original input and completed steps; null omits a key. Keys must be disjoint from config. |
| `interactive` | boolean | no | — | — | — | Whether this dispatch is a CONVERSATION rather than a single run (ADR-129 D9). An interactive dispatch ends each turn by SUSPENDING RATHER THAN COMPLETING: the adapter writes a contentless suspending declaration, the run parks at paused:awaiting-interactive-turn carrying neither a question nor a predicate, and everything that arrives while it is parked drains into the next dispatch in arrival order. Runtime-facing and daemon-read, exactly as a tool's mcp_servers block is: it never transits binding_config, so the dispatched program neither has to understand it nor gets to disagree with it. The binding must OFFER what this REQUESTS — the tool declares in_flight { yields_turn = true } — and a request against a binding that does not offer it is refused at load naming both files and both lines, because a dispatch that quietly ran one-shot would be discovered by a person whose chat ended after one message. Default: false, and the dispatch is byte-identical to one built before this attribute existed. |
| `attended` | block | no | — | — | — | Whether this dispatch is ATTENDED: one process in a terminal its person attaches to (ADR-179 D2). Declared on a work_order_type's own capability or select recipe, which lowering copies onto its synthesized step; an authored workflow step declaring it is refused at load. At most one of it and interactive. Default: absent, and the dispatch is byte-identical to one built before this block existed. |

## `step.ask` block

Nested under `step`.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `question` | string | yes | — | — | — | The question a person is asked, in the words they will read. Required. It rides the Work Order's pause context, so it is what work_order.get, work_order.tree and 'tera workorder tree' render. |
| `context` | string | no | — | — | — | Optional structured evidence beside the question, as a JSON **object** — written as a string, normally a heredoc, the same way input_schema and output_schema are. It rides the pause context under the context key, the same shape human.ask writes. |
| `description` | string | no | — | — | — | Optional informational label for this question — what the step is asking about. It rides the pause context and the parked record so an operator reading a parked Work Order can tell which step of a long workflow is asking. |
| `to` | string[] | no | — | — | — | The principals being asked, as authenticated principal identifiers (ADR-117 D12). Optional: an ask that names nobody parks exactly as an ask always has, waiting for an operator's 'tera workorder answer', and a deployment that enrolls nobody keeps working. RECIPIENTS ARE EXPLICIT ONLY — none is ever inferred from the principal that requested the work or from the work-order type's configuration. The To is a set, so a repeated entry is refused; an empty entry is refused. No entry's spelling is parsed or validated beyond that (PRD-021 SC10). |
| `to_groups` | string[] | no | — | — | — | The GROUP CLAIMS being asked, as authenticated group/role claim strings (ADR-118 D10). A separate attribute from 'to' because a group must be named explicitly: addressing is over opaque authenticated identifiers, so no prefix or namespace inside 'to' means 'group' (PRD-021 SC10). Each claim expands, when the question is delivered, to every ENROLLED principal whose LAST AUTHENTICATED identity carried it — an EXPANSION over the enrollment store, never the group's membership, and stale by construction: somebody who has not authenticated since joining is not in it, and somebody who left is until they authenticate again. Expansion is bounded: at most 8 group addresses per ask, 64 principals per group and 128 distinct expanded principals, each refused by name rather than truncated. Combine freely with 'to'; the two resolve into one deduplicated recipient set and every member is put through the deployment's inbound-acceptance policy identically. BEING REACHED BY A GROUP IS NEVER A GRANT — whoever answers is authorized independently (ADR-118 D6). The list is a set, so a repeated entry is refused; an empty entry, or one with leading or trailing whitespace, is refused. No entry's spelling is parsed beyond that. |
| `urgency` | integer | no | — | — | — | The sender's claim about this question's importance, 1–5 ascending: 1 whenever, 2 routine, 3 notable, 4 urgent, 5 interrupt-me-now (PRD-021 §11). It is a claim, never a delivery guarantee — the recipient's own per-endpoint reachability floors decide what is pushed where, and neither side overrides the other's half. Orthogonal to whether an answer is needed: an ask always needs one, whatever its urgency. Omit for the deployment's default. |
| `timeout` | string | no | — | — | — | How long this question is live, as a Go duration ("45s", "2h"). It is the ONE deadline (ADR-117 D8): how long delivery keeps trying, how long a window keeps offering the interaction, and when the wait ends are all derived from it, and there is deliberately no second clock to declare. Omit for an unbounded wait, which is the default and is how an ask has always behaved. A non-positive value is refused rather than honoured — a wait woken before it waited for anything is not a wait. The instant it resolves to rides the parked row, so a daemon restart re-arms the same moment instead of starting the duration again. |
| `on_silence` | string | no | — | — | — | What the deadline passing MEANS: the value this step's output takes when the timeout elapses with nobody having replied (ADR-117 D8). It must be an answer the response contract could actually have received — one of a choice's options, true or false for a confirm, any text for a text contract — because silence stands in for an answer, and a value no recipient could have chosen is one the run would carry forward regardless. A DECLINE IS NOT SILENCE: an explicit refusal to answer is a reply, it settles the question, and it never takes this value. Requires timeout, since silence with no deadline never arrives. Omit to have an elapsed deadline fail the step into the exit funnel instead. |
| `response` | string | no | — | — | — | What shape of answer is wanted, as a JSON **object** written as a string (normally a heredoc, the same way output_schema is): {"kind": "choice", "fields": [{"name": "decision", "type": "enum", "options": ["unlock", "deny"]}]}. The kind is one of "ack", "confirm", "choice", "text", "form" and the field types are "string", "number", "boolean", "enum" — closed and FLAT, because flatness is what lets every contract degrade to a numbered text prompt on a carrier with no buttons (ADR-117 D14, ADR-119 D2). A "confirm" may additionally declare {"decision": {"polarity": "approve_on_true"}} (or "approve_on_false"), which makes it a CLOSED GOVERNANCE DECISION: the settled question's outcome — approved, refused, declined or cancelled — is then kept on the record clock, so a deployment can still tell an approval from a refusal after the message body has aged out (ADR-117 D10 Amendment 1, PRD-021 §16). The polarity is DECLARED and never inferred, because a confirmation's polarity is the sender's rather than the kind's — "Cancel the pending unlock?" answered true is a refusal — and the prompt that fixes the reading is content the record does not outlive. It is legal on "confirm" alone, its boolean field must be required, and it carries a polarity and nothing else; an ask that declares none is unchanged and keeps attribution plus digest only. The grammar is closed at every level, so a key it does not name is refused wherever it appears — including inside the decision: an ask RETURNS A VALUE and has nowhere to put a capability reference, a handler or any other verb (ADR-118 D6, PRD-021 §8), and nowhere to put a second deadline (ADR-117 D8). Nullable: omit it for a question whose answer is constrained by this step's output_schema alone. It is what the FAR SIDE IS OFFERED; output_schema is what this run ACCEPTS. |
| `artifact` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | An ADR-107 artifact this question carries, by REFERENCE — never bytes, which are neither stored on the message row nor written into a recipe field (PRD-021 §17/§18). Repeat the block for several, in the order a recipient sees them; at most 16 per ask, and a repeated 'from' is refused. Requires 'to' or 'to_groups': an unaddressed ask is never delivered, so an attachment on one reaches nobody. Authority is checked at TWO seams and neither subsumes the other. At ADMISSION, before the message is stored, the deployment decides whether this sender may share each handle — the ask declares the ASKING RUN as the share's scope and marks the share restricted, so it is authorized against that run's custody and never against the daemon's own management grants; a handle the run may not share refuses the whole send, and the question is then simply not delivered, leaving the run parked and answerable by 'tera workorder answer' exactly as an undeliverable ask always has been. At DELIVERY, resolution happens PER WINDOW and is gated first by that window's content class (ADR-118 D9) and then by the artifact channel's own availability answer (ADR-107) — so a terse endpoint resolves nothing at all, a carrier declaring attachment_carriage = "none" is delivered the message without the attachment, and a reference the channel will not describe is omitted from that window alone. Being shown an attachment is never an authorization: whoever answers is authorized independently (ADR-118 D6). |

## `step.ask.artifact` block

Nested under `step.ask`. Repeatable.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `from` | string | yes | — | — | — | Where the ADR-107 artifact handle comes from: a CEL expression over this run's own state, in the SAME namespace input_map reads (input, steps, outputs, retry) — for example steps["capture"].output.handle or input.snapshot. Required, and there is deliberately NO literal-handle form: a handle is random and minted at publish time (ADR-107 D3), so a literal in a recipe could only name an artifact that does not exist yet and will not exist when the recipe runs. It must evaluate to a NON-EMPTY STRING at the moment the run parks; anything else fails the step into the exit funnel rather than delivering the question without the evidence the author attached to it. Because the expression can read only this run's state, an ask can reference exactly the artifacts the run was already handed — there is no enumeration verb, and no handle enters from outside the run. |
